title: Regular Saunas Could Help Us Cope with Heat Waves
paragraphs: As heat waves become more frequent in many parts of the world, scientists are looking for ways to help people cope with extreme temperatures. According to several recent studies, spending time in a sauna or a hot bath on a regular basis may help prepare the body for hot weather.

The idea is based on a process known as heat acclimation. Athletes have long trained in hot conditions to prepare for competitions in hot regions. According to Jari Laukkanen, a cardiologist at the University of Eastern Finland, similar changes in the body can also occur through passive heat exposure, such as sitting in a sauna or a hot bath.

When the body is regularly exposed to heat, it gradually adapts. Sweating starts earlier and becomes more efficient, blood flow to the skin improves and the volume of blood plasma increases. As a result, the heart and blood vessels are put under less strain, making it easier for the body to control its temperature in hot weather. A systematic review of 16 studies found that the most effective way to prepare is to spend at least 30 minutes in the heat on six to seven days in a row. Changes in the body begin after a few days, and full adaptation usually takes one to two weeks.

Interestingly, the benefits may not only be physical. Dr. Jessica Mee of the University of Worcester, who is studying whether regular hot baths improve heat tolerance, has found that people who are used to the heat also tend to drink more regularly, pace themselves better and recognize warning signs earlier.

However, experts stress that saunas should be used to prepare for summer, not as a way to cope during a heat wave. During extreme heat, the body is already under stress, and extra heat could increase the risk of heatstroke. In addition, people with fevers, serious heart conditions or very low blood pressure should avoid saunas and hot baths.

It is also important to note that most of the studies were carried out in laboratories, so it is not clear whether the results apply to everyday sauna use. Experts say that drinking plenty of fluids and avoiding activity during the hottest hours remain the most important ways to stay safe.
